Q: Accessing implicitly-created arrays A:

storage_ points to an array of std::bytes and, AFAIU, under current standard wording, reinterpret_cast<T*>(storage_) still does as far as the compiler is concerned (https://eel.is/c++draft/expr.reinterpret.cast#7 does speak about actual object but of pointer type).
You just need to respect alignment (which you do).
Using std::launder, the compiler does not know anymore what you are doing with the pointer. As far as it is concerned again, it gets back the memory location of a T. And it happens to be the one pointed by storage_. It is only well defined if there is actually a T object is living there (the precondition you mentioned: https://eel.is/c++draft/ptr.launder).

So this is the correct way to access the objects within the storage.
Note: there are discussions to remove the need for this std::launder in your situation: https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2024/p3006r1.html

Now you are right to distrust your construct_at call.

Merely do: std::construct_at(reinterpret_cast<T*>(storage_) + size_, t);

It is equivalent to ::new (static_cast<void*>(storage_)+ size_) T(t); (https://eel.is/c++draft/specialized.construct#3)

So there is no need for a possibly invalid std::launder there.

Side note: I'm unsure if you are getting a proper array of T with data() (which would allow for pointer arithmetic) or if you merely get access to the first T object. https://eel.is/c++draft/allocator.requirements.general#36 seems to imply that the answer is yes:

[Example 1: When reusing storage denoted by some pointer value p, launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(new (p) byte[n * sizeof(T)])) can be used to implicitly create a suitable array object and obtain a pointer to it. — end example]

But this point is disputed (see comments and the link you found yourself https://github.com/cplusplus/draft/issues/4553).

It might be more accurate then to do: auto data() noexcept { return *std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T(*)[Capacity]>(storage_)); }

And in either case, you still have to start the lifetime of the elements (as you do), except if T is an implicit lifetime type.

Q: proper way to nest sheet presentations, while having a foreground/background cycle not pop everything back to the root view A:

Just be aware that showing sheets over sheets is not in conformance with Apple's User Interface Guidelines, ref. their recommended Best Practices for sheets:

Display only one sheet at a time from the main interface. When people close a sheet, they expect to return to the parent view or window. If closing a sheet takes people back to another sheet, they can lose track of where they are in your app. If something people do within a sheet results in another sheet appearing, close the first sheet before displaying the new one. If necessary, you can display the first sheet again after people dismiss the second one.

So with regard to your question:

What is the correct pattern for using NavigationStacks when you have arbitrarily-deeply-nested sheets?

There is no correct pattern, because Apple doesn't want you to do it this way.

See also SwiftUI: Nested sheets dismissed on app background with TabView + NavigationStack + .navigationDestination (iOS 26).

Q: KeyError: 0 in if clause? A:

I now figured out why I got this error. I created this dataframe by removing some rows based on column values of an existing dataframe. Therefore, I did not have continuous index values starting at 0. Therefore, I reset the index and then everything worked out because I then got a continuous index.
